analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice awards, limits expert testimony, and shortens the time to sue over medical injuries.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in March 2009 and never received a hearing, floor vote, or Senate consideration before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten medical malpractice law nationwide. It would cap the money a patient can win for pain and suffering at $250,000 per doctor and $500,000 total per hospital chain, limit total recovery in a death case to $1.4 million per doctor, require an expert report within 120 days or the case is dismissed, and let only actively practicing physicians testify against other doctors. It would also shorten filing deadlines, shift court costs onto patients who turn down settlement offers and then win less at trial, and shield doctors and hospitals from liability for unpaid emergency care unless they were grossly negligent.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, hospitals, nursing homes, and medical malpractice insurers. Damages caps and stricter expert rules would reduce the size and number of malpractice payouts, which is the largest input to malpractice insurance premiums. The bill also specifically protects malpractice insurers from paying more than the doctor's policy limit when the insurer rejects a settlement offer — a rule that today can leave insurers on the hook for the full judgment.

how_it_helps.text: Caps non-economic damages (pain and suffering, loss of companionship) at $250,000 from all liable doctors combined and $500,000 from all liable institutions combined, regardless of how many are responsible or how severe the injury [S2][S3].
Caps total damages from any single doctor in a wrongful death case at $1.4 million, adjusted for inflation — including punitive damages [S3].
Requires a written expert report within 120 days of filing; failure means the case is dismissed with prejudice and the patient pays the defendant's attorney fees [S3].
Bars anyone but an actively practicing physician from testifying about the standard of care, cutting off retired doctors and non-physician experts commonly used by injured patients [S3].
Lets doctors and hospitals shift their attorney fees and expert costs onto patients who reject a settlement offer and then win less than 80% of it at trial [S3].
Gives full immunity to providers giving unpaid emergency care unless the negligence was willful, wanton, or worse [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured or killed by medical negligence. The caps fall hardest on people whose injuries cause little lost income — children, retirees, and stay-at-home parents — because their losses are mostly non-economic. Cost-shifting and short filing deadlines (2 years for adults, no tolling for children under 12 until age 14) would end valid cases before families understand what happened to them.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap is a fixed number regardless of injury severity: a child brain-damaged for life and an adult with a temporary injury get the same maximum for pain and suffering, and juries are instructed not to even consider the cap when deciding what the harm was worth [S3].

The 120-day expert report requirement, the ban on non-practicing-physician experts, and cost-shifting would make many legitimate cases too risky or expensive for families and their attorneys to bring [S3].

Supporters' argument: malpractice litigation drives defensive medicine and insurance costs, and caps would lower premiums and healthcare spending; the bill also preserves full recovery of economic damages like medical bills and lost earnings, and the Good Samaritan immunity encourages volunteer emergency care [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real policy debate here: some economists link malpractice litigation to defensive medicine, and doctors in high-premium states pushed hard for caps. But the burden of this bill lands on the people least able to bear it — families of children, elderly patients, and others whose losses are mostly non-economic — and it stacks procedural hurdles (expert reports, practice-requirement for experts, cost-shifting, 2-year deadlines) on top of the caps. It is designed to reduce payouts more than to improve care.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2009 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess (R-TX), himself a physician, introduced the Medical Justice Act of 2009 on March 12, 2009 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day — its only action [S5].
Eight House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4].
The bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote, and Congress ended January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients and the trial lawyers who represent them keep today's full right to sue, uncapped; doctors, hospitals, and malpractice insurers get no new protections.

for.name: Michael C. Burgess
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medical Justice Act of 2009 and became its only named sponsor

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership (Chair John Conyers Jr.)
against.role: Chair, House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote after its referral; the bill died in committee

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's nine supporters was a House Republican; the Democratic majority that controlled the Judiciary Committee never acted on it, and no Democrat cosponsored.

industries.note: Caps and settlement rules would directly cut the payouts these insurers owe, and the bill would strip away the existing rule that an insurer which unreasonably rejects a settlement can be forced to pay a judgment above the doctor's policy limit — a protection for patients that this bill deletes. Their savings come straight out of compensation to injured patients.

Damage caps, proportionate liability, expert-qualification rules, and cost-shifting would lower malpractice exposure and premiums for doctors and their business entities, which the bill defines broadly to include physician-owned companies. The savings come at the price of full compensation for patients they harm.

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and long-term care facilities
industries.note: The bill caps non-economic damages from all institutions combined at $500,000 and extends shorter deadlines and expert rules to nursing homes, home health agencies, and hospices, reducing their liability in injury and death cases.

Expert-report deadlines, dismissal with fee awards, the practicing-physician rule for experts, and cost-shifting would shrink the volume and economics of malpractice cases. Their interest in this bill runs with their clients',' the injured patients.'
